title: Why It Seems Like Great White Sharks Are Overrunning Maine
author: Molly Taft
text: Lifeguard Greg Wilfert was swimming off the coast of Scarborough, Maine, in August when he was yanked underwater by a force tugging on his rescue buoy. Wilfert, a lifeguard of 55 years, told local news outlet WFSB that he first thought he’d gotten caught on a boat propeller, but the real culprit was a great white shark.The incident is one in a long line of great white sightings off the coast of Maine this year. It was a busy summer for shark sightings along the rest of the East Coast, but Maine, in particular, seems to have had a great white bonanza. A dozen sightings were reported in a two-day period near Pine Point Beach in southern Maine in August. Beaches were temporarily closed all over the state following multiple sightings throughout July and August. The sharks followed beachgoers through the end of summer: A great white was spotted off Wells Beach over Labor Day weekend, while a fisherman caught another on the holiday about 30 miles down the coast.WIRED's Guide to How the Universe WorksYour weekly roundup of the best stories on health care, the climate crisis, new scientific discoveries, and more.The waters off the coast of Maine are some of the world’s fastest-warming, and the Atlantic has seen a series of marine heat waves. The El Niño weather phenomenon is only boosting global heat further. But experts told WIRED that the reason for our recent glut of shark encounters is a lot more complicated than just attributing them to climate change, especially when it comes to great whites. Instead, a successful conservation effort decades ago is likely starting to pay dividends, coupled with more people bringing technology that can spot sharks to the beach.Featured VideoSharks Are Not Eating the InternetWhen Steven Spielberg’s classic movie Jaws came out in 1975, great whites were in trouble. The species had declined in waters off both the east and west coasts of the US thanks to overfishing, bycatch, and trophy hunting. In the 1990s, federal protections were instated for both the sharks and for gray seals, one of their key prey species.Maine’s state shark monitoring system uses a technology called acoustic telemetry, which outfits the animal with a tag that emits a unique electronic signature. Underwater stations can then pick up on that signal and log the tagged sharks, helping track their movement up and down the coast. Maine’s program is less than a decade old, and “not every shark is tagged,” says Matthew Davis, a shark expert at Maine’s Department of Natural Resources. That makes pinpointing exactly what is going on with this uptick in sightings a little more challenging.But Davis and Walter Golet, an associate professor at the University of Maine School of Marine Science who collaborates on shark research, both believe that there were more great whites off the coast this summer compared to decades past. They attribute it in part to federal protections working. Great whites males take 26 years to reach adulthood, while females can take up to 33 years. That timeframe aligns with when federal protections were put in place and could help explain why more sharks are showing up off of Maine. Research generally backs this up: Multiple studies have found that protections for both sharks and seals helped to increase populations along the East Coast.While climate change has driven massive changes in the ocean, including pushing many species northward as waters warm, its direct effect on great white sharks is a little more murky. Some research has suggested that great whites could suffer from very hot ocean temperatures by causing them to overheat and forcing them to slow down or move to colder water to seek food. But James Sulikowski, the director of the Coastal Oregon Marine Experiment Station at Oregon State University, emphasizes that great whites can control their body temperature, which enables them to withstand much larger ranges in ocean temperatures than other shark species.You’ve read your last free article.The intersection of technology, power, and culture. Prey species may “hang around a little bit longer because the water is going to be a little bit warmer,” he says, which could mean great whites spend more time in areas they previously would’ve been in for only a few months.Another indirect impact of climate change: more people at the beach during hot days. And, since it’s 2026, more and more people bring equipment, from iPhones to hobby drones, that can capture high-quality footage of marine life. All three experts say that the raft of shark sightings in Maine this summer may just be a result of people going outside with better, more technologically advanced eyes on the ocean.“There are more of them, but they are also easier to see, so you have to untangle that,” says Golet. “I think we’re all sort of a prisoner of our own timeline.”
